Could You Live on a Planet Orbiting a Dead Star?

Episode 64 of a daily journey through the universe. 💫
In 1992, Aleksander Wolszczan and Dale Frail found the first confirmed planets beyond our solar system, orbiting pulsar PSR B1257+12, a dead star spinning about 160 times a second and bathing its worlds in deadly radiation.

segments.text: The first planets ever found beyond our Sun orbit a dead star. Could anything live there?
For centuries, people wondered if other stars had planets. The first answer was a surprise.
segments.headline: Do other stars have planets?

segments.text: In nineteen ninety-two, two astronomers, Aleksander Wolszczan and Dale Frail, were studying a pulsar with the giant Arecibo radio telescope.
segments.headline: Arecibo, 1992

segments.text: A pulsar is a spinning neutron star, the dead core of an exploded star. It sweeps beams of radio waves across space, like a lighthouse.
segments.headline: A cosmic lighthouse

segments.text: This one spins about one hundred sixty times every second.
Its ticks were incredibly regular, but not perfectly. Tiny wobbles in the timing revealed something tugging on the star: planets.
segments.headline: Tiny wobbles

segments.text: They were the first planets ever confirmed beyond our solar system.
But you wouldn't want to visit. These worlds are blasted by radiation from the pulsar. Probably no place for life.
segments.headline: No place for life

segments.text: How do planets survive a star exploding? Maybe they formed afterward, from the wreckage.
segments.headline: Born from the wreckage?
